title: Session 1 - Participant 37 User + Claude/Protégé Behavior Graphs
goal: Produce a clause-by-clause statutory compliance analysis of a residential solar home improvement contract and its accompanying financing agreement against California and federal disclosure requirements, delivering (a) a clause comparison sheet mapping each statutory requirement to the contract's treatment of it, and (b) a short analytical memorandum of findings in the form the participant would send to a supervising attorney.
context:
I work as a consumer protection case analyst and paralegal on residential solar and home-improvement disputes. My core task is contract compliance analysis: taking a signed home improvement contract and its associated financing agreement, and testing them clause by clause against the statutory disclosure requirements that govern that kind of sale in California. Where a contract falls short — a missing cancellation notice, an unitemised price, no translated copy where the sale was negotiated in Spanish — that gap becomes the foundation of the homeowner's claim. The output of my analysis goes to a supervising attorney, who decides how to proceed.

For a non-expert: a solar company sells a homeowner a system, usually door-to-door, financed over twenty-plus years. California law requires specific things to appear in that paperwork, in a specific form, and requires the homeowner to be told they can cancel within three days. My job is to read the paperwork very closely and identify exactly which of those requirements were not met, with a page and clause citation for each one, so nothing I report back is guesswork.

For this session I am running that same analysis on publicly available contract templates and published statutory sources rather than client files, so there is no confidentiality issue with screen recording. The methodology is identical to what I do on live matters; only the inputs change.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not:
Yes — both deliverables were produced within the hour: a completed clause comparison sheet and an analytical memorandum ready for attorney review.
That said, achieving the goal required considerably more correction of the legal content than I expected. Claude's statutory analysis contained recurring inaccuracies: requirements stated in terms the statute does not use, citations attached to the wrong subdivision, and confident assertions about what a provision required that did not survive checking against the primary source. The workflow held together because verification was built in as a separate, human-only stage (Step 5) rather than folded into drafting. Had I written the memo straight from the model's output, several findings would have been wrong on the law.
So the goal was met, but the collaboration was more supervisory than collaborative on the substance. The value was in structure, speed and coverage — organising the requirement matrix, running a first pass across every row, producing a memo skeleton — not in the legal analysis itself, which I had to supply and repeatedly correct.

Step 1.step_action: I locate a publicly available residential solar home improvement contract and a matching consumer solar financing agreement (from a state consumer agency publication, a regulator's sample filing, or a vendor's published template) and save them locally as the working document set. I then ask Claude to identify which bodies of law govern a door-to-door residential solar sale in California, so that I have a defined scope before I start reading - statutory, regulatory, and federal.
Step 1.input: Two downloaded PDFs (solar HIC template, consumer solar loan agreement template); my prompt describing the transaction type (residential, owner-occupied, negotiated at the home, financed).
Step 1.output: A local folder of source PDFs plus a scoping list naming the governing authorities to be tested — (codes to be confirmed) Bus. & Prof. Code §7159 (home improvement contract content), §7159.5 (down payment and progress payment limits), §7169 (Solar Energy System Disclosure Document), Civ. Code §§1689.5–1689.14 (home solicitation sales and the three-day right to cancel), Civ. Code §1689.7 (form and delivery of the cancellation notice), Civ. Code §1632 (foreign-language translation), Civ. Code §1770 (CLRA), TILA and Regulation Z (12 C.F.R. pt. 1026) for the credit disclosures, and the FTC Cooling-Off Rule (16 C.F.R. pt. 429).
Step 1.tools: Free version: Google Chrome, Adobe Acrobat Reader, Google Drive, Paid version: Claude Max
rubrics: The scoping list separates California state authority from federal authority rather than merging them
Every authority is cited to a specific code section, not a general statute name
The list includes at least one solar-specific provision (not merely generic home improvement law)
No authority is cited that has been repealed, superseded, or does not exist
Each authority is accompanied by a one-line statement of what it actually requires, so the list is usable as a checklist rather than a reading list

ratings.output_quality_reason: The scoping list was well-organised and immediately usable — state and federal authority were kept apart, solar-specific provisions were identified rather than collapsed into generic home improvement law, and each entry carried a short statement of what the provision requires, so the list functioned as a checklist rather than a reading list. The problem was accuracy at the level of the citation itself. Several provisions were cited to the section but attached to the wrong subdivision, and at least one requirement was described in terms the statute does not actually use. Those errors were only caught in Step 5, when I read the sections in lexis. A scoping list that reads well but sends you to the wrong subdivision is worse than one that is merely incomplete, because it invites reliance. Structure earned a high mark; reliability did not.

goal_achievement.Why or why not:
Yes. A complete, well-structured scoping list was produced quickly and it set the frame for the whole workflow. But it could not be relied on without independent verification, so what it completed was the organising work, not the legal work

Step 2.step_action: Working from the Step 1 scoping list, I build a requirement matrix in Google Sheets: one row per discrete statutory obligation, with columns for the authority, the precise requirement, where in the contract it should appear, and how a violation would present. I use Claude to convert the statutory text into discrete testable obligations, then edit the matrix myself to remove duplication and add requirements Claude did not break out.
Step 2.input: The Step 1 scoping list; statutory text pulled in Step 5 where already available.
Step 2.output: solar_compliance_matrix — a requirement matrix of roughly 25–35 discrete testable obligations.
Step 2.tools: Free version: Google Sheets,Paid version: Claude Max
rubrics: Each row states one obligation only; compound requirements are split
Each row is traceable to a subdivision of the statute, not just the section
The matrix distinguishes content requirements (what must be said) from form requirements (typeface, placement, number of copies)
The matrix flags which obligations are strict-compliance and which permit substantial compliance
No obligation is stated in terms that cannot be tested against a document

ratings.output_quality_reason: The decomposition of statutory text into discrete testable obligations was the single most useful thing produced in the session. Compound requirements were split correctly, content requirements were kept apart from form requirements, and the matrix arrived in a state I could edit rather than rebuild. I removed some duplication and added obligations that had not been broken out — particularly on the form side, where typeface and placement requirements were initially folded into content rows. Not a 5 because the strict-compliance versus substantial-compliance distinction was applied inconsistently, and that distinction matters a great deal to how a finding is later characterised.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Yes — the matrix was structurally sound and saved substantial time. My edits were refinements rather than corrections

Step 3.step_name: Extract and index the contract clauses
Step 3.step_action: I read the home improvement contract in full and index its clauses - identifying the price and payment terms, scope of work, cancellation provisions, warranty and performance language, and any integration or arbitration clause. I upload the contract to Claude and ask for a structured clause inventory with page and section references, then check that inventory against the document myself to confirm nothing was invented or missed.
Step 3.output: A clause inventory listing every substantive provision with its location in the document, verified against the source.
Step 3.tools: Free version: Adobe Acrobat Reader, Google Docs,Paid version: Claude Max
rubrics: Every listed clause carries a page and section reference that resolves correctly in the source PDF
No clause appears in the inventory that is not in the document
The inventory captures boilerplate and back-page terms, not only the front-page commercial terms
Provisions are quoted or paraphrased accurately without softening or strengthening the actual language
Where a clause is ambiguous, the ambiguity is preserved rather than resolved by assumption

ratings.output_quality_reason: This was the weakest output in the session and the step that generated the most rework. The clause inventory looked complete and well-organised, but the extraction itself was not reliable: references did not consistently resolve to the right place in the source, and provisions were paraphrased in ways that drifted from the actual contract language — sometimes resolving an ambiguity by assumption, sometimes stating a term more firmly than the document does. Because the inventory is the input to every subsequent step, I could not proceed on it until I had cross-checked it clause by clause against the source document and, for the statutory provisions it referenced, against Westlaw. That cross-checking is exactly the work the step was meant to save. An extraction output that is subtly wrong is more expensive than no extraction at all, because it looks finished.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: No — a usable clause inventory existed at the end of the step, but it was mine after correction, not the model's. The output as delivered could not be relied on.

Step 4.step_name: Run the clause-by-clause comparison and populate the comparison sheet
Step 4.step_action: I work down the requirement matrix and, for each obligation, record whether the contract satisfies it, partially satisfies it, or omits it, citing the clause relied on. I use Claude to run a first pass across the matrix and then correct its findings against the document - this is the step where I expect the most disagreement between us and where my own judgement does the most work.
Step 4.input: solar_compliance_matrix.xlsx, the Step 3 clause inventory, both source PDFs.
Step 4.output: completed clause comparison sheet with a compliance determination and supporting citation for every row.
Step 4.tools: Free version: Google Sheets, Paid version: Claude Max
rubrics: Every determination cites the specific contract clause it rests on, or expressly records that no clause addresses the requirement
"Partial compliance" determinations state precisely what is missing
No determination rests on an inference from silence unless the statute makes silence itself the violation
Findings supported by the document are kept separate from observations that would need further evidence to confirm
Where the correct determination depends on facts outside the document (e.g. the language of the oral sale), the row is marked as fact-dependent rather than resolved

ratings.output_quality_reason: Once it was working from a corrected clause inventory, the comparison ran well. The first pass caught most of the defects in the specimen — including the down payment exceeding the statutory cap and the front-loaded progress payment schedule — and populated every row rather than leaving gaps. It missed a few, which I found myself, and a small number of determinations rested on inference from silence where the statute does not make silence itself the violation. Not a 5 because I still had to check each row, but the corrections here were refinements rather than repairs, which was not true of Step 3.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Yes — full coverage of the matrix with determinations that were mostly sound, and the misses were the kind I would expect to catch on review.

Step 5.step_name: Verify the statutory basis in Lexis and Protégé
Step 5.step_action: I take every authority relied on in the comparison sheet and pull the current text in Westlaw or Lexis, checking the effective date, any recent amendment, and the citing references for judicial gloss on the requirements. Nothing Claude asserted about the law goes into the memo until I have read the section myself. This step is deliberately run without Claude.
Step 5.input: The authority column of the completed comparison sheet.
Step 5.output: A verified authority list with current statutory text, effective dates, and any correction to the compliance determinations made in Step 4.
Step 5.tools: Free version: N/A, Paid version: Westlaw, LexisNexis
rubrics: Every authority relied on has been opened and read in a primary source database
The version checked is the version in force at the relevant date
Any authority that turns out to be misstated or inapplicable is struck from the analysis rather than reworded
At least one interpretive authority (case or regulatory guidance) is identified for the cancellation and translation requirements
Corrections arising from verification are carried back into the comparison sheet, not held separately

ratings.output_quality_reason: This step was run without Claude by design, so the rating reflects my own verification work rather than an agent output. Every authority relied on was opened and read in a primary source database, effective dates were confirmed, and the corrections surfaced here were carried back into the comparison sheet rather than held separately. This step is also what makes the rest of the workflow defensible — the errors from Steps 1 and 4 were caught here and nowhere else.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: N/A — no agent involvement in this step. That was deliberate and I would keep it that way.

Step 6.step_name: Focused analysis - cancellation notice and Civil Code s71632 translation
Step 6.step_action: I return to two requirements that carry disproportionate weight in this practice area and analyse them in depth: whether the cancellation notice satisfies the form, content, timing and duplicate-copy requirements, and whether the transaction would trigger the s71632 obligation to deliver a translated contract where the sale was negotiated primarily in Spanish. I use Claude to pressure-test my reading and to argue the opposing position, then decide the point myself.
Step 6.input: The cancellation provisions from the source contract; verified statutory text from Step 5; a stated factual assumption that the sale was negotiated door-to-door in Spanish.
Step 6.output: A written analysis of both requirements, including the counterargument a defendant would raise and my assessment of it.
Step 6.tools: Free version: Google Docs, Paid version: Claude Max, Westlaw
rubrics: The cancellation analysis addresses form, content, timing and delivery separately
The §1632 analysis identifies the trigger conditions and states which are assumed rather than established
A genuine defence argument is stated at its strongest, not as a straw man
The remedy consequence of each defect is identified, not just the defect
My conclusion is stated with a confidence level rather than asserted flatly where the point is contestable

ratings.output_quality_reason: Asking the model to argue the opposing position was the most productive use of it in the session. The defence arguments it produced on the cancellation timing point were ones I would want to be ready for, and stating them at their strongest sharpened my own conclusion rather than softening it. The form/content/timing/delivery breakdown was handled properly. Marked down because the §1632 analysis did not cleanly separate the trigger conditions I was assuming from those the documents established, and I had to impose that distinction myself.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Yes — adversarial testing of a position is something the model does well, and it is a use where the accuracy problem matters less because I am evaluating the argument rather than relying on it.

Every finding cites both the contract clause and the statutory provision
The memo states what the documents do not establish as clearly as what they do
No conclusion appears in the memo that is not traceable to a verified source

But I rewrote most of the prose. The draft explained concepts an attorney reader would not need explained, hedged where the analysis was actually firm, and in places asserted conclusions more confidently than the verified record supported. Useful as a skeleton, not as a draft. The memo that went out was mine.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Yes — a complete memo in the right shape was produced within the time available. The structure was the contribution; the content was mine.
